gallery.description: This view of the rising Earth greeted the Apollo 8 astronauts as they came from behind the Moon after the fourth nearside orbit. On the Earth 240,000 miles away, the sunset terminator bisects Africa.

gallery.title: File:Crab Nebula.jpg
gallery.artist: NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll (Arizona State University)
gallery.credit: A Giant Hubble Mosaic of the Crab Nebula
gallery.description:
This is a mosaic image, one of the largest ever taken by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, of the Crab Nebula, a six-light-year-wide expanding remnant of a star's supernova explosion. Japanese and Chinese astronomers recorded this violent event in 1054 CE.
The orange filaments are the tattered remains of the star and consist mostly of hydrogen. The rapidly spinning neutron star embedded in the center of the nebula is the dynamo powering the nebula's eerie interior bluish glow. The blue light comes from electrons whirling at nearly the speed of light around magnetic field lines from the neutron star. The neutron star, like a lighthouse, ejects twin beams of radiation that appear to pulse 30 times a second due to the neutron star's rotation. A neutron star is the crushed ultra-dense core of the exploded star.
The Crab Nebula derived its name from its appearance in a drawing made by Irish astronomer Lord Rosse in 1844, using a 36-inch telescope. When viewed by Hubble, as well as by large ground-based telescopes such as the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope, the Crab Nebula takes on a more detailed appearance that yields clues into the spectacular demise of a star, 6,500 light-years away.

The newly composed image was assembled from 24 individual Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 exposures taken in October 1999, January 2000, and December 2000. The colors in the image indicate the different elements that were expelled during the explosion. Blue in the filaments in the outer part of the nebula represents neutral oxygen, green is singly-ionized sulfur, and red indicates doubly-ionized oxygen.

gallery.title: File:Path to Totality in Cleveland (53650459062).jpg
gallery.artist: LASZLO ILYES from Cleveland, Ohio, USA
gallery.description:
Despite our usual gray skies here in Cleveland, OH, we were graced with somewhat clear viewing during the total solar eclipse on May 8th, 2024.

This composite is created from images taken through my 9.25" Schmidt-Cassegrain Telescope and a Canon EF 200mm L II lens x2 Extended using my Canon EOS 5D Mark III. 

Sadly, I missed capturing the details of solar prominence in 64Mp detail during totality, but three and a half minutes doesn't give you very much time to get all the images you want. 

I'm just grateful to have experienced this in my lifetime.

gallery.title: File:Solar eclipse on April 8, 2024 in Québec city, pano no mirror version.jpg
gallery.source: Solar eclipse on April 8, 2024 in Québec city, pano no mirror version
gallery.description: The solar eclipse on April 8, 2024, also known as the Great North American Eclipse, was a total solar eclipse visible across a swath covering parts of North America, from Mexico to Canada and traversing the contiguous United States. During this event, a partial solar eclipse was observed in Québec City. The image captures a solar eclipse from an elevated observation point in Quebec City on a notably windy day. A photographer, equipped with specialized gear, documents the astronomical event. He uses a camera fitted with a 100-400mm lens and a 2X extender, effectively providing an 800mm focal length on a full-frame format. To secure the special graduated filter for the eclipse, which initially did not fit, he resorts to using tape. The image shows the tripod reinforced with metal stakes and a counterweight to combat the strong wind and minimize vibrations. The final composition results from multiple manual shots of the partial eclipse, continually adjusting the camera towards the sun to keep the Sun and Moon aligned due to the Earth's movement. The images, developed in Lightroom for basic corrections, are combined into a single composition in Photoshop, highlighting significant phases of the eclipse.

gallery.title: File:Insolation during the 2024 Eclipse (SVS5248 - penumbra 20240408 185700).jpg
gallery.description: The obscuration dataset used to calculate insolation. Obscuration, the fraction of the Sun's area covered by the Moon, is calculated at 10-second intervals from 15:42:10 to 20:52:20 UTC at a resolution of 360/8192 degrees per pixel (roughly 3.75 × 4.9 km at 40°N). The maps are global equirectangular projections centered on (0°, 0°), with white = 100% obscuration and black = 0%. The sharp borders are the terminator (the day-night line). The complete dataset can be downloaded as a single .zip file (194 MB).
